catalog_quote: Word accent (stress) is marked by an acute ´. Accent placement is a problem in itself. For the dialect he describes, Wedekind 1980 gives the rule that a word-final syllable is stressed if it has a long vowel, otherwise stress falls on the penultimate, e.g. gogáa 'skin' vs. máala 'meat'. I found this rule corroborated by most (though not all) of my examples from Marsabit. On the other hand, Hayward (p.c. and forthcoming) claims that stress always falls on the penultimate (at least in nouns), regardless of the quantity of the final vowel. This is also what Straube heard from his informants in most cases. It may well be that differences in stress placement are among the dialectologically relevant isoglosses within Burji.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the final syllable when that syllable contains a long vowel; otherwise it falls on the penultimate syllable (gogáa 'skin' vs. máala 'meat'). Sasse found this rule (from Wedekind 1980) confirmed by most of his own Marsabit data; Hudson 1989: 6 states the same rule as general for all five Highland East Cushitic languages including Burji. A competing report (Hayward, and Straube's informants) has fixed penultimate stress in nouns regardless of final-vowel length, which Sasse attributes to dialect difference.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Sasse: rule corroborated by 'most (though not all)' Marsabit examples; Hayward and Straube's informants: always penultimate (at least in nouns). Hudson 1989: 6 marks stress in entries only where the rule is violated, 'not uncommonly on word-final short vowels', which he suspects are phonemically (or historically) long. Voith 2020: 16 (citing Wedekind 1990: 52-53): pitch is tied to stress and not phonemic.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on citation forms (dictionary lemmas; nouns cited in accusative in Hudson). Sasse's own data are from emigrant Burji at Marsabit, Kenya (1977), 'of unidentifiable dialectal provenience', influenced by Borana Oromo and Swahili; Wedekind's rule is for 'the dialect he describes' (Ethiopia); Hayward's informant was from the Soyyaama (Highland) area. The scanned text layer renders the acute-accented vowels of gogáa / máala as '&'; the page image was checked and shows gogáa, máala.
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Burji proper (burj1242), also called Dhaashatee by its speakers (Voith 2020). Sasse 1982's own stress data come from emigrant Burji at Marsabit, Kenya, of 'unidentifiable dialectal provenience'; Wedekind 1980's rule is for an Ethiopian dialect; Hayward's penult-only claim is from a Soyyaama (Highland) speaker. Voith 2020 distinguishes Highland and Lowland Dhaashatee (mutually intelligible, mostly phonological differences); no separate glottocodes exist for these dialects in our record. Sasse suggests stress placement may itself be a dialect isogloss.

sources.note: §5 pp. 17-18: stress marked by acute; Wedekind 1980's rule = final syllable stressed if it has a long vowel, otherwise penult (gogáa 'skin' vs máala 'meat'); corroborated by most but not all of Sasse's Marsabit data; Hayward (p.c.) says always penult in nouns; Straube's informants mostly penult; stress placement may be a dialect isogloss.

sources.note: §3.1.5 'Stress', p. 16 (PDF p. 24), second-hand: 'According to Wedekind (1980: 138), stress in Dhaashatee is fully determined by phonological rules. It falls on the last syllable, except in words ending on a short vowel, where the penultimate syllable is stressed. Contrary to other Cushitic languages spoken in the area, such as Afar, Saho, or Borana-Oromo, pitch is tied to stress and not phonemic (Wedekind 1990: 52-53).' No first-hand stress data; fieldwork Feb 2020 in Dilla and Soyama, mostly Highland Dhaashatee.

Burji) a general rule of stress on word-final long vowels and (rarely) diphthongs, otherwise on the next-to-last syllable; stress is marked in the entries only where this rule is violated, 'not uncommonly on word-final short vowels', which may be phonemically long.
